title: Balls of Fury
full_review:
"Balls of Fury" (Rogue) follows the comic fortunes of a washed-up pingpong prodigy named Randy Daytona (Dan Fogler). Having disgraced himself as a teenager at the 1988 Olympic Games, Daytona ekes out a living as a stunt pingpong performer in Reno, Nev., until he is approached by FBI agent Rodriguez (George Lopez).

Rodriguez asks Daytona to help the FBI catch a mysterious and powerful crime lord named Feng (Christopher Walken), who also happens to be a rabid fan of Daytona's sport. Since Feng was responsible for killing Daytona's father (Robert Patrick) over a gambling debt incurred when Daytona lost at the Olympics, the former champ quickly overcomes his initial doubts and agrees to do what he can.

Feng, Rodriguez explains, now holds secret pingpong tournaments to which he invites only the best players. The plan to catch him thus depends on Daytona's ability to receive such an invitation, which eventually comes in the form of a golden paddle.

Daytona has become rusty since his days of early prowess, so Rodriguez places him under the tutelage of Wong (James Hong), a blind master of the sport. Wong's daughter, Maggie (Maggie Q) -- also a prodigiously gifted player -- soon becomes Daytona's practice partner, with predictable romantic results.

Frequently crude and always preposterous, "Balls of Fury," directed and co-written by Ben Garant, has some flashes of comic originality. Walken's Feng, for instance, is a bizarre amalgam of early Dracula, late Elvis and a 6-year-old. And how can one fail to feel at least some affection for a film in which the archvillain's first line of dialogue is: "Okey-dokey, artichokey"?

The script by Garant and Thomas Lennon, who also get in some good satiric swipes at everything from kung fu movies to 1980s heavy metal music along the way, never takes itself seriously, reveling in its own silliness, though too often straying from the path of good taste. As for the slapstick, it's strictly anything for a laugh, including such questionable conceits as the sight gag of Siamese twins with a paddle in each hand playing a solitary opponent.

"Balls of Fury" is thus a little too furious and a little too frantic for its own good. By the time it's over, viewers are apt to feel more exhausted than amused.

The film, though acceptable for older adolescents, contains much crude language, one instance of profanity, suggestive gestures, gross and scatological jokes, and mild gay-themed humor. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
